answer:
To determine which integer is not in the range of \( f(x) \), we analyze the function \( f(x) \) defined as follows:

- For \( x > -2 \), \( f(x) = \left\lceil \dfrac{1}{x+2} \right\rceil \)
- For \( x < -2 \), \( f(x) = \left\lfloor \dfrac{1}{x+2} \right\rfloor \)

**Case 1: \( x > -2 \)**

Here, \( x + 2 > 0 \), so \( \dfrac{1}{x+2} \) is positive. The ceiling function \( \left\lceil \dfrac{1}{x+2} \right\rceil \) rounds up to the nearest integer. As \( \dfrac{1}{x+2} \) can take any positive value from just above 0 to infinity, the ceiling function will yield all positive integers \( 1, 2, 3, \ldots \).

**Case 2: \( x < -2 \)**

Here, \( x + 2 < 0 \), so \( \dfrac{1}{x+2} \) is negative. The floor function \( \left\lfloor \dfrac{1}{x+2} \right\rfloor \) rounds down to the nearest integer. As \( \dfrac{1}{x+2} \) can take any negative value from just below 0 to negative infinity, the floor function will yield all negative integers \( -1, -2, -3, \ldots \).

Combining both cases, the range of \( f(x) \) includes all positive and negative integers. However, \( \dfrac{1}{x+2} \) can never be zero, and thus \( f(x) \) can never be zero. Therefore, the integer not in the range of \( f(x) \) is \( 0 \).
